https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: NEW YORK—Large, growing budget deficits and rising public debt-to-GDP ratios in advanced economies are rattling markets. With interest rates on government debt having gone from near zero (and even negative, in some cases) to much higher levels, rising short- and long-term bond yields have cast doubt on the sustainability of some public debts and led many to ask if a crisis might be looming.

LONDON—Brazil has an unfortunate habit of disappointing. Despite the country’s exceptional natural-resource endowment, its growth trajectory resembles what Brazilians call the flight of a chicken (voo de galinha): a brief flutter followed by an inevitable fall back down to Earth. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise re-election raises the risk of another letdown.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.byline: Robert Muggah and Ilona Szabó de Carvalho
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: SÃO PAOLO—Until President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva staged a remarkable comeback to win re-election, no Brazilian presidential candidate had overturned a first-round defeat in a runoff. Lula did so with nearly 52% of the vote, against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48%. More than 128 million Brazilians turned out—nearly three million more than in the first round.

SHANGHAI—My search for truth inside China has been stymied. Banned from the China Development Forum (CDF), after participating for 25 years as the longest-attending foreign delegate, I feel like an outsider in what was once the country’s most prestigious international gathering. Deteriorating relations with former friends in Hong Kong, some of whom avoid eye contact with me now, have not helped matters. In both cases, I was cut off after offering constructive criticism—highlighting structural malaise in the mainland economy and a loss of autonomous identity in Hong Kong—the essence of what we call debate in the West.

BERKELEY—Six Nobel laureate economists recently signed an open letter supporting Proposition 40, California’s Billionaire Tax Act, which, if passed by a simple majority of voters, would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of an estimated 250 individuals with a net worth exceeding $1 billion who resided in California on January 1, 2026. We believe the proposal is poorly designed and likely to do more harm than good.

ISTANBUL—Today’s economic growth depends heavily on AI investment and fiscal spending. The International Monetary Fund estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual global growth over the next decade, raising the average rate from 3% to 3.5%.

NEW DELHI—This has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars—from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today—a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order. Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.

CAMBRIDGE—Is China booming or stagnating? On one hand, its export industries—including electric vehicles, solar panels, and virtually the entire range of manufactured goods—are the envy of the world, and its tech and AI industries are second only to the United States, with Europe trailing far behind. On the other hand, as I have written many times, China is now in the sixth year of a full-blown, Japan-style real-estate crisis. Could China be booming and stagnating at the same time?

RIO DE JANEIRO—Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil’s presidential election is a blow to Donald Trump’s plan for the Western Hemisphere. The US president was hoping to huddle with client states to the south who mimic his business and mano dura (iron fist) posturing, while further betraying liberal partners. That plan, within reach until Sunday’s vote, is now in tatters.

PRINCETON—The postwar architects of European integration notoriously relied on crisis conditions to build more extensive institutions. By contrast, for incremental, piecemeal reforms to succeed, the challenges Europe faces must be relatively small. That hardly describes Europe’s current predicament.

BERLIN—On February 24, 2027, it will have been five years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in flagrant violation of international law. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s neo-imperialist adventure—his “special military operation”—was supposed to be a brief and decisive war of conquest. But it soon became apparent that he had underestimated his victim. The Ukrainians have been determined to defend themselves, whatever it takes, and for a while, they could count on a united West, with the United States and Europe standing together in providing military and civilian support.

OXFORD—Two tumultuous elections have captured headlines this week. In Brazil, incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated his far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. And in Serbia, the student-led opposition ousted Aleksandar Vučić after 14 years in power. But the challenge for these new governments is just beginning. Whether they like it or not, both will be swept up in the global scramble for critical minerals and metals.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.byline: Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: WASHINGTON, DC—The most concrete outcome from last month’s summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was an apparent agreement to set up a US-China AI incident-reporting channel. But even if either government proves willing to use this direct line or start sending data across the Pacific, they must first address a more pressing issue: US and Chinese frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they would need.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.byline: Gordon LaForge and Robert C. Orr
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: WASHINGTON, DC—The warnings about the safety of frontier AI models continue to grow louder. Writing in Time in early October, the former chief scientist of the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute put the probability of us all dying because of smarter-than-human AI systems at 50%. On the same day, a senior OpenAI employee announced that he had left the company because of its “broken” safety culture. But the United States has shown no interest in regulating the technology, except for a “morally binding” voluntary accord recently signed by tech CEOs and US President Donald Trump.

JAKARTA—When the energy transition confronts difficult economic conditions within a country, addressing the transition’s unequal impact becomes both more challenging and more imperative. In Indonesia, with an economy recently described as a “ticking time bomb,” coal mining has long been the main driver of GDP in certain regencies and provinces. Pursuit of the energy transition in such places raises the tricky political question of how to support economic diversification, and boost economic growth, in these areas while also combating climate change.

The answer may seem obvious: reducing vulnerability to economic shocks caused by the shift away from fossil fuels requires broadening income sources. But that is easier said than done. A just energy transition requires a wider transformation that includes creating meaningful job opportunities, closing human-capital gaps, and alleviating poverty. Most importantly, these efforts must be highly localized to account for each area’s unique strengths and each community’s specific needs.

Pulau Panggung, a village located in Muara Enim, one of Indonesia’s most coal-dependent regencies, in South Sumatra province, illustrates this vulnerability starkly. According to research by WALHI Sumatera Selatan (Friends of the Earth South Sumatera) and the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law, 56.7% of the village’s residents are employed as mine workers, including casual laborers. When coal mining arrived in the early 1990s, the community largely abandoned farming, its main economic engine at the time. Now, as mining firms face expiring contracts and begin implementing efficiency measures, villagers’ livelihoods are under threat, but this time without a ready-made substitute.

The village’s post-coal economy could return to agriculture and embrace nature-based tourism. But shifting to these sectors requires a healthy ecosystem, making it essential to force companies to fulfill their obligations to restore mined land. Moreover, because villagers gave up farming decades ago, they would need training in sustainable agriculture techniques and opportunities to develop skills for other alternative livelihoods, such as digital-based marketing.

Some of the barriers to creating new livelihoods in Pulau Panggung are structural, such as the ambiguous legal status of land, a long-standing problem across Indonesia. But the bigger challenge, both here and elsewhere, is the lack of formal channels for developing effective local initiatives. Each village’s strengths must serve as the foundation for community-based economic transformation. Unfortunately, Indonesia’s top-down policymaking and regulatory regime, particularly in the energy sector, hinders efforts to maximize local strengths.

The Indonesian government directs transition planning by providing general guidance, which provincial and regency plans should theoretically elaborate on, identifying what is unique to each place. Yet the 2025–2029 South Sumatra medium-term regional development plan gives no clear direction on how economic transformation will be carried out, only that efforts to move away from a coal-based economy remain suboptimal. The plan recognizes that natural resources must play a role but does not explain how to use them in a way that fits the needs of each village and avoids harming ecosystems.

This problem is not unique to Indonesia. Many other governments have similar gaps in their energy-transition policies. The key is for policymakers to enable a more bottom-up approach by focusing on two objectives.

First, policymakers must directly involve affected communities. Entrusting transition planning to local governments and giving communities a genuine role in the decision-making process would help officials and companies design tailored interventions that expand employment opportunities for workers at risk of displacement.

Embedding community-driven initiatives in these policies must begin with local assessments. Before any plan is approved, the government should conduct participatory mapping of livelihoods, land status, workforce skills, and local strengths. In Pulau Panggung, this kind of mapping would highlight its agricultural and tourism potential.

Second, policymakers should explore the possibility of a regional fund that could redirect government revenue derived from mining and fossil-fuel production toward supporting community-based transitions. One model to follow is the Alaska Permanent Fund, whereby the state government invests a portion of its oil and mining revenues for the long-term benefit of all current and future Alaskans.

Managed by a state-owned corporation, this sovereign wealth fund helps finance public services like education, health care, and basic infrastructure. Policymakers, in both developed and developing countries alike, can use such a vehicle to ensure a sustainable economic transition by operating transparently and allowing local communities to direct the proceeds toward their chosen priorities.

Time is running out to establish regional endowment funds. Policymakers in Indonesia and other countries must act before mining and fossil-fuel revenues stop flowing. As a first step, they can run pilots in affected regions—like Muara Enim—to show what is possible. Waiting too long risks leaving these communities with a plan but no capital to implement it.
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.bio: Grita Anindarini is a senior strategist at the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: CAMBRIDGE—Last month, the Nobel laureate economist Paul Krugman gave a talk at the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, which focused on geoeconomics. The term refers to countries’ ability to exploit economic interactions for geopolitical ends. Think of China’s threats to cut off trading partners from its exports of rare-earth minerals.

MADRID—At first glance, the wave of student-led protests that has swept across France might resemble the events of May 1968. Both featured surging crowds of demonstrators calling for education reform, criticizing the government, erecting blockades, and being confronted by riot police. Both also attracted casseurs, who turn protest into destruction. But whereas the students of 1968 were seeking to overturn the established order, today’s protesters want the established order to deliver for them.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.byline: Mariana Mazzucato and Anna Hope Emerson
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: LONDON—Governments around the world say they have no room to act. Although inequality and the cost of living are rising, fiscal space, we are told, is tight. Yet in many cases, the squeeze is self-imposed. It follows from equating fiscal responsibility with cutting deficits and debt, rather than with building an economy’s capacity to grow, withstand shocks, and meet its obligations over time. In fact, cutting spending in a weak economy can leave the debt-to-GDP ratio higher, not lower; and when fiscal rules bite, public investment is often the first thing cut.

VIENNA—After 14 years of authoritarian rule, Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have been ousted from power. Although polls had predicted a close election, the student-led opposition ultimately won by a wide margin. In an election that was neither free nor fair—owing to media capture, violence against the government’s opponents, and the SNS’s blatant misuse of state resources—the Student List won 53% of the popular vote, which translated into 141 parliamentary seats and an absolute majority. Vučić and his SNS trailed badly, with 38.8% and 103 seats.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/onpoin.byline: Danielle Keats Citron and Ari Waldman
https://www.project-syndicate.org/onpoin.body: CHARLOTTESVILLE/IRVINE—Around the world, civil rights and civil liberties are coming under profound threat, and that threat has a name: selective privacy. The powerful enjoy it, while vulnerable groups, protesters, and others who stand up to power do not. The slogan writes itself: “Privacy for me, but not for thee.”
